a: Existentialism is a philosophical movement that emphasizes individual existence, freedom, and choice. It emerged in 19th-20th century Europe, with key figures including Søren Kierkegaard, Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Paul Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir, and Albert Camus. The core idea is 'existence precedes essence' — humans are born without predetermined purpose and must create their own meaning through choices. Key concepts include radical freedom (we are 'condemned to be free' and responsible for our choices), bad faith (denying our freedom by blaming circumstances), authenticity (living according to our own values), the absurd (the conflict between our search for meaning and the universe's indifference), and existential dread (anxiety from confronting freedom's responsibility). Sartre wrote 'Being and Nothingness' (1943) and 'Existentialism is a Humanism' (1946). Camus explored the absurd in 'The Myth of Sisyphus' (1942) and 'The Stranger' (1942). Beauvoir applied existentialism to feminism in 'The Second Sex' (1949). Existentialism differs from nihilism (which denies all meaning) and essentialism (which believes humans have fixed natures).

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is a widely used, evidence-based psychotherapy developed by Aaron Beck in the 1960s. CBT is based on the cognitive model: our thoughts influence our feelings, which influence our behaviors. The core idea is that psychological problems arise from distorted or unhelpful thinking patterns and learned behaviors. CBT helps patients identify, challenge, and replace negative automatic thoughts and cognitive distortions (such as all-or-nothing thinking, catastrophizing, overgeneralization, and personalization). Key techniques include cognitive restructuring (examining and changing thought patterns), behavioral activation (engaging in positive activities), exposure therapy (gradually facing feared situations), journaling (tracking thoughts and behaviors), and skills training (problem-solving, relaxation). CBT is typically short-term (12-20 sessions) and goal-oriented. It has been proven effective for depression, anxiety disorders, PTSD, OCD, eating disorders, and insomnia. CBT has strong empirical support from hundreds of randomized controlled trials. It has also been adapted into dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) for borderline personality disorder and acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT).

Art movements are distinct styles or philosophies shared by artists during specific periods. Major movements include: Renaissance (14th-17th c., realism, perspective, humanism — Leonardo, Michelangelo), Baroque (17th-18th c., drama, emotion, Caravaggio, Bernini), Neoclassicism (late 18th c., classical ideals, Jacques-Louis David), Romanticism (early 19th c., emotion, nature, Delacroix, Turner), Realism (mid 19th c., everyday life, Courbet), Impressionism (1870s-80s, light and color, Monet, Renoir, Degas), Post-Impressionism (1880s-90s, emotional expression, van Gogh, Cézanne, Seurat), Fauvism (1905-7, bold colors, Matisse), Expressionism (early 20th c., emotional experience, Munch, Kandinsky), Cubism (1907-14, geometric forms, Picasso, Braque), Futurism (early 20th c., speed, technology), Dada (1916-24, anti-art, absurdity, Duchamp), Surrealism (1920s-30s, unconscious mind, Dalí, Magritte), Abstract Expressionism (1940s-50s, spontaneous expression, Pollock, Rothko), Pop Art (1950s-60s, popular culture, Warhol, Lichtenstein), Minimalism (1960s-70s, simplicity, Judd), and Contemporary (1970s-present, diverse, global).

The digestive system breaks down food into nutrients the body can absorb and use. Digestion begins in the mouth, where teeth chew food and saliva (containing amylase) starts breaking down carbohydrates. The esophagus moves food to the stomach via peristalsis. The stomach uses hydrochloric acid and the enzyme pepsin to break down proteins into amino acids, churning food into chyme. The small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) is where most digestion and absorption occurs. The pancreas releases enzymes (trypsin, lipase, amylase) and bicarbonate to neutralize stomach acid. The liver produces bile (stored in the gallbladder), which emulsifies fats. The small intestine's villi and microvilli absorb nutrients into the bloodstream. The large intestine (colon) absorbs water and electrolytes and forms stool. The rectum stores stool, and the anus expels it. Common digestive disorders include acid reflux, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, and celiac disease. The gut microbiome (trillions of bacteria) plays a crucial role in digestion, immune function, and even mental health through the gut-brain axis.

The human brain is the body's most complex organ, containing about 86 billion neurons. Major regions include the cerebrum (largest part, divided into two hemispheres and four lobes: frontal — reasoning, planning, movement; parietal — touch, spatial awareness; temporal — hearing, memory, language; occipital — vision), the cerebellum (coordination, balance, fine motor control), and the brainstem (medulla oblongata, pons, midbrain — controls basic life functions like breathing, heart rate, and sleep cycles). The limbic system (including the hippocampus — memory formation, amygdala — emotion, and hypothalamus — homeostasis) processes emotions and memories. The basal ganglia coordinate movement. The corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres. Neurons communicate through electrical impulses and chemical neurotransmitters (dopamine — reward, serotonin — mood, acetylcholine — learning, GABA — inhibition). Neuroplasticity allows the brain to reorganize itself throughout life. The brain uses about 20 percent of the body's energy despite being only 2 percent of body weight. Key brain disorders include Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, stroke, epilepsy, depression, and schizophrenia.
